about.tagline: A hardware profiler for Linux. What CPU-Z, GPU-Z and HWMonitor do on Windows, in one native program: what machine you have and what it is doing right now.

bat.health.hint: How much of the factory capacity is left. Below 80 % it shows in runtime; that is normal after some 500 cycles.
bat.left.hint: At the current draw. Idle lasts far longer than compiling, and both figures are true.
bat.limit.hint: Your laptop can avoid charging all the way. Stopping at 60 or 80 % noticeably extends cell life if the machine stays plugged in.
bench.card.title: Benchmark
bench.compare.title: Previous runs on this machine   ·   {signo}{pct}% against the one from {fecha}
bench.cond.endfreq.tip: The average over the last stretch. If it is well below the peak, the processor did not hold its top clock through the run.
bench.cond.load.tip: What was keeping the machine busy right before starting. With background load the result cannot be compared.
bench.cond.maxload.tip: The most another program took while measuring. A fifteen-second run per workload takes two and a half minutes: something waking up halfway through does not show in the figure above, which is taken before starting.
bench.dialog.clear.body:
{n} {plural} from this machine will be deleted.

This cannot be undone.
bench.dialog.delete.body:
«{nombre}» will be deleted.

This cannot be undone.
bench.dialog.duration.body:
How many minutes each of the ten measurements lasts.

The whole run takes ten times this.
bench.dialog.name: Name of the run
bench.dialog.name.body: So you remember what changed between one and the next:
bench.dialog.name.tip: Give it a name: «new thermal paste», «summer»…
bench.drift.cooler: This run peaked {grados} °C below the median of the {n} previous {pruebas} with the same score. If you have just cleaned it or repasted it, this is where it shows.
bench.drift.hotter: This run peaked {grados} °C above the median of the {n} previous {pruebas} with the same score. That is usually dust or dried-out thermal paste — or simply a warmer room, which no sensor in the machine measures.
bench.duration.tip:
How long each of the ten measurements lasts: five loads, on one thread and on all of them. The whole run takes ten times this.

Longer ones do not give a higher score: they give the one that holds up once the machine is already warm.
bench.explain.scaling:
Scaling
How much performance multiplies when using every thread. It never reaches the thread count: the ones sharing a core split the same execution units.
bench.history.note: Only from this machine and only on disk: nothing is sent anywhere. Comparing against numbers off the internet hardly ever helps, because they were measured with another governor and another temperature; comparing against yourself does tell you whether something changed.
bench.history.oldscale: {n} of these runs were measured before the benchmark was fixed and with a different scale, so they have no score: their figure would not mean the same as today's. Everything else they recorded is still there.
bench.intro: Measures the processor with five different loads, first on one thread and then on all of them. The interesting part is not just the number: each load scales differently, and that shows what makes use of the threads and what sits waiting on memory. While it runs, the machine goes flat out.
bench.quick.tip: Eight seconds instead of twenty. Enough to get an idea, but with less room for the turbo to settle.
bench.score.above: {pct} % above what is usual for this part. The {n} recorded measurements range from {min} to {max}.
bench.score.alone: There are no measurements of this processor to compare against yet. The table fills up with the ones people send in.
bench.score.below: {pct} % below what is usual for this part. The {n} recorded measurements range from {min} to {max}.
bench.score.normal: It performs as expected for this part. The {n} recorded measurements range from {min} to {max}.
bench.score.onlyown: This figure compares against your own runs of the same length, but not against other machines: that needs the {s} s measurement, which is the only one taken the same way everywhere.
board.tip.bios: The «System BIOS Release» field of the SMBIOS table. Not the version the maker publishes on its site, but the one the firmware declares about itself.
board.tip.chipset: The full name pci.ids uses for the LPC/eSPI bridge on bus 0, which is what acts as the chipset.
board.tip.memctl: On modern processors it is built into the CPU itself, not the chipset.
cache.l3.uneven: The L3 is not the same across the processor: {reparto}.
cache.l3.vcache: That is the V-Cache stacked on just one of the two chiplets: a thread that lands on the big one gets more out of memory.
caches.line.note: The smallest unit that travels between memory and cache. Reading a single byte pulls in the whole line, which is why walking contiguous data is far faster than jumping around memory.
caches.map.note: Each block is one physical cache instance; its width is the logical CPUs that share it.
caches.subtitle: {n} distinct caches over {nucleos} cores and {hilos} threads
caches.ways.note: An N-way cache stores each address in one of N possible places. More ways reduce clashes between data competing for the same set, at the cost of a more expensive lookup.
clock.turbo.capped: The kernel caps it at {actual} of the {max} the silicon can do
clock.turbo.off: Turbo is off: the silicon would reach {max}
core.name: core {n}
core.spread: the weakest one (core {n}) tops out at {pct}% of the best
core.spread.type: the weakest one (core {n}) tops out at {pct}% of the best of its kind
cpu.best.legend: {nucleos}{hilos}: the ones the firmware says came out best of the wafer, and where the scheduler sends single-threaded work. {reparto}.
cpu.power.headline: {pct} % of {w} W
cpu.power.none: this machine does not publish it
cpu.subtitle: {nucleos} cores · {hilos} threads · {sockets} socket{s}
cpu.tip.voltage: What the processor asks for in its current state. With turbo on, the chip's own microcontroller takes over and the real value goes above this; what actually arrives is measured by the board regulator, when its chip labels the channels.

disk.warn.backup: the power-loss backup memory has failed
disk.warn.life: It has {pct}% of its life left, by its own wear counter.
disk.warn.media.many: {n} pieces of data that could not be read since it left the factory.
disk.warn.media.one: {n} piece of data that could not be read since it left the factory.
disk.warn.pmr: its persistent memory region is unreliable
disk.warn.readonly: it has switched to read-only mode
disk.warn.reliability: the drive has downgraded its own reliability
disk.warn.spare: the spare area has dropped below the maker's threshold
disk.warn.temp: the temperature is outside the range it accepts
disk.warn.unknown: The drive is flagging a problem (code {codigo}).
gpu.codec.name: Codec
gpu.engine.name: Engine
gpu.na.integrated: Voltage regulators and the fan belong to a separate card: this one is powered and cooled along with the rest of the machine.
gpu.na.novram: An integrated GPU has no memory of its own: it uses the system's, so there is no type, bus, bandwidth, data rate or Resizable BAR to report.
gpu.na.novram.clocks: With no video memory of its own there is no memory clock to show.
gpu.na.novram.sensors: With no memory chips of its own there is no memory temperature or voltage.
gpu.tip.bandwidth: How much data fits through the bus in a second: the memory rate times the bus width. It limits a card before raw compute power does.
gpu.tip.compute: Each vendor counts them its own way and they are not equivalent: one AMD compute unit groups dozens of the cores NVIDIA counts one by one.
gpu.tip.datarate: The real speed the data travels at. It is not the clock: GDDR6 at 1258 MHz moves sixteen transfers per cycle, that is 20 Gbps.
gpu.tip.hotspot: The hottest point on the die, always above the edge temperature. It is what drives the fan.
gpu.tip.memeff: The clock the data travels at, which is the one spec sheets advertise. Memory moves several transfers per cycle of its command clock.
gpu.tip.rebar: With Resizable BAR the CPU sees the whole card memory at once. Without it, it only reaches a 256 MB window that the driver has to keep moving, which costs performance. It is enabled in the BIOS, and both the board and the card have to support it.
gpu.tip.rops: The ROPs, which write the finished pixels into the final image.
gpu.tip.shared: GTT: system RAM the driver lends the card when VRAM runs short. It is not graphics memory, which is why it goes separately.
gpu.tip.state: Whether the firmware is cutting performance back, and why. It explains a game running worse than it should while the card looks far from its limits.
gpu.tip.videouse: The video encode and decode engines, which work separately from the rest of the GPU.
gpu.tip.visible: How much VRAM the CPU can address at once.
gpu.tip.vr: The regulators feeding the die. They are not in hwmon: the card's own microcontroller reports them.
guard.cpu.fix: The interface works again with the last series built for plain x86-64:
guard.cpu.meanwhile: In the meantime this works without Qt, and dumps all the hardware to the terminal:
guard.cpu.missing: This processor is missing instructions the installed Qt needs: {banderas}
guard.cpu.override:
If you think this is wrong (some distributions build their Qt for plain
x86-64) {variable}=1 skips this check.
guard.cpu.why:
Qt {mayor}.{menor} and later require them, which leaves out Intel chips older than 2008
and AMD chips older than 2011. Nothing is wrong with your machine.
home.tagline: What hardware you have inside and what it is doing right now. Everything is read from the system itself: no data leaves this machine.
mem.channel.same: All {n} modules sit on the same channel. Split across two, the memory would move twice as much per second.
mem.channel.single: There is only one module, so memory runs at half its bandwidth. A matching second module in the other channel doubles it; on a machine with integrated graphics that shows up in the frame rate more than almost anything else.
mem.mixed: The memory runs at {actual} MT/s and cannot go past {lento}, which is what the slowest module gives. Another one claiming {rapido} changes nothing: they all share one clock, so the set settles at the slowest.
mem.title: {tam} of memory
mem.underclocked: The memory runs at {actual} MT/s of the {rated} it claims to support. That is usually the fast profile (XMP or EXPO) left off in the BIOS, though it can also be the processor's official limit.
memory.bw.capped: Careful: this way of measuring tops out at {techo} on this machine, so your memory may be faster than that figure says.
memory.bw.hugecache: This processor's cache is so large that getting past it would ask for more memory than a program like this should reserve.
memory.bw.intro: Measures how much memory actually moves, reading a block larger than the cache. Takes a tenth of a second.
memory.bw.nocache: This processor's cache is too small to measure on its own: below a megabyte what gets timed is the call, not the memory.
memory.bw.nomem: Not enough free memory to measure without pushing something to swap.
memory.bw.note: MT/s tell you what the module is rated for, and the theoretical figure is a multiplication. This is what the machine actually achieves when reading: none reach their theoretical figure, and below half there is usually an unpopulated channel.
memory.elev.alreadyroot: The program already runs as administrator but the SMBIOS table could not be read.
memory.elev.helper: The helper that gets launched only knows how to read that table and a few processor registers: it runs no commands and writes nothing.
memory.elev.nopkexec: pkexec is not installed, so there is no way to ask for permissions.
memory.elev.nopkexec.hint: It comes with the distribution's polkit package. Running the whole program as root works too.
memory.elev.smbios: Module detail lives in the SMBIOS table, which the kernel reserves for the administrator because the machine serial numbers sit alongside those fields.
memory.elev.spd.many: The {n} modules above come from their own SPD chips, which read without permissions. Each one's capacity, which slot it sits in, how many are free and what speed the BIOS set them to are in the SMBIOS table, which the kernel reserves for the administrator.
memory.elev.spd.one: The module above comes from its own SPD chip, which reads without permissions. Each one's capacity, which slot it sits in, how many are free and what speed the BIOS set them to are in the SMBIOS table, which the kernel reserves for the administrator.
memory.lat.noexec: This system does not allow executing memory reserved on the fly, which is how latency is measured.
memory.lat.note: How long an access takes when the processor cannot get ahead of it. It is what you feel when jumping around scattered data structures, and buying more memory does not improve it: it depends on the silicon and the timings.
memory.lat.nox86: Latencies are measured with a fragment of machine code that only exists for x86-64.
memory.lat.partial: RAM could not be measured: this processor's cache is so large that the chain of accesses needed does not fit in a reasonable time.
memory.lat.title: Latency by level
memory.spd.note: The SPD is a chip every module carries with its own specifications. It says what speed it can run at, while the BIOS decides the one it actually runs at: without XMP enabled it stays on JEDEC's conservative values.
memory.spd.read.many: {n} modules read from their SPD chips
memory.spd.read.one: {n} module read from its SPD chip
memory.tip.chips: Who made the silicon, which is often not who sells the module. The SPD says it, not the SMBIOS table.
memory.tip.elevate:
Launches a minimal helper through polkit that only knows how to read the SMBIOS table and a few processor registers.
It runs no commands and writes nothing.
memory.tip.firmware: The BIOS writes it as {mts} MT/s; same grade, rounded the other way. That is the number dmidecode shows.
memory.tip.module: SPD chip at {address} on the i2c bus. Without the SMBIOS table there is no telling which board slot it sits in, so these are numbered in reading order.
memory.tip.profiles: Timings the manufacturer guarantees above the JEDEC ones. They are detected, but their formats are not public and their figures are not decoded: guessing them would be making them up.
memory.tip.rated: What the module claims it can do, according to its own SPD chip.
memory.tip.running: Running at {actual} MT/s of the {rated} it supports. It may be an XMP profile left off, or the processor's official memory limit, which on many models sits below what the modules can take.
memory.tip.size: Worked out from the module's own SPD chip.
net.none.body: No interface has a route to the network.
net.units.note: The same traffic is either 116 MB/s or 931 Mb/s: speed tests use bits.
note.hardware: This machine does not expose it
note.platform: Does not apply to this platform
pcie.now: Running at {actual}; the card and the slot can do {max}
perm.dialog.title: Permanent permissions
perm.installed: Permissions installed: the password will be asked once per session.
perm.nopython.install: there is no system Python to install with
perm.permanent.tip:
Installs the helper system-wide with its own polkit authorisation.
After that the password is asked once per session, not on every launch.
It needs the password once to install it.
prov.apis.none: There is no OpenGL, Vulkan or OpenCL library to ask.
prov.apis.none.hint: Usually a machine with no graphical environment installed. The driver brings them: mesa, vulkan-radeon, vulkan-intel or the NVIDIA package.
prov.bat.nosysfs: The kernel does not publish power supply state.
prov.bat.nosysfs.hint: /sys/class/power_supply is missing; that is where the battery and charger come from.
prov.cppc.nobase: This machine does not publish its base clock by any route.
prov.cppc.nobase.hint: CPUID leaf 0x16 is Intel Skylake onwards, ACPI CPPC needs the firmware to declare it, and this processor's brand string carries no frequency.
prov.cppc.nobclk: The reference clock (BCLK) cannot be known without root.
prov.cppc.nobclk.hint: Only CPUID 0x16 on modern Intel or the processor's MSRs give it. Deriving it from the base clock is only reliable on ACPI CPPC platforms, where it is 100 MHz.
prov.cpu.nofreq: The kernel does not expose the current per-CPU frequency.
prov.cpu.nofreq.hint: Some governors and kernels without cpufreq do not publish it.
prov.cpu.nofreq.vm: The hypervisor does not expose the processor frequency.
prov.cpu.nofreq.vm.hint: The host governs the clock: there is no cpufreq to read inside a virtual machine.
prov.cpu.nosysfs.hint: Only happens on systems that are not Linux.
prov.cpuid.failed.hint: The environment forbids executing anonymous memory. /proc/cpuinfo will be used instead.
prov.cpuid.nodb: No identification database has been generated.
prov.cpuid.nosocket.hint: A rule can be added in silux/db/sockets.json.
prov.cpuid.notx86: CPUID is an x86 instruction; this machine is not x86.
prov.cpuid.notx86.hint: On ARM the identity is read from /proc/cpuinfo.
prov.cpuid.unknown: This processor is not in the database ({marca}).
prov.cpuid.unknown.hint: Rebuild the database with tools/gen_cpu_db.py or add an entry.
prov.crashed.hint: This is a silux bug, not your machine's. It deserves a report.
prov.denied.hint: The system will not allow access to that path as this user.
prov.disk.health: Drive diagnostics are kept by each drive in its own counters.
prov.disk.health.hint: With permissions you see power-on hours, terabytes written and the wear on each one.
prov.dmi.noboard: The BIOS does not publish the board model.
prov.dmi.noboard.hint: Some manufacturers leave the field blank on purpose.
prov.dmi.none: This machine exposes no DMI information.
prov.dmi.none.hint: Happens on simple virtual machines and on many ARM boards.
prov.drm.inteldriver.hint: The kernel does not publish occupancy counters for this graphics either, which is where usage comes from on other Intel parts. The clocks, the monitors and what Vulkan and OpenGL declare do come out.
prov.drm.intelhw.hint: The DRM node carries no hwmon and its performance counter has no thermal event, so there is nowhere to get it from. What the kernel does count — per-engine usage and, on integrated parts, the watts — is already being read.
prov.drm.intelroot: Graphics usage and power are kept in kernel counters, which do not read without permissions. This Intel graphics does not publish its temperature.
prov.drm.intelroot.hint: With permissions you get per-engine usage and, on integrated parts, the watts. Temperature does not come out by any route; the clocks, the monitors and what Vulkan and OpenGL declare do come out without asking for anything.
prov.drm.inteltemp: This Intel graphics does not publish its temperature.
prov.drm.metricsnew: This card reports telemetry in version {version}, which this program does not read yet.
prov.drm.metricsnew.hint: Throttling reasons, voltages and regulator temperatures come from there. The layout moved between versions and reading it with the previous positions would give believable, wrong numbers, so they are left out. The version is in the report: with a dump from a machine like this one it can be added.
prov.drm.nodriver: The kernel has no driver for {tarjeta}: it is falling back to the basic framebuffer.
prov.drm.nodriver.hint: The card is identified through the PCI bus, but with no driver there are no clocks, no temperature, no power draw and no memory. This happens when booting with nomodeset, with the driver not installed, or with a card newer than the kernel.
prov.drm.nogpu: No graphics card is registered with the kernel.
prov.drm.nogpu.hint: Happens on servers with no video output and in virtual machines with no emulated graphics.
prov.drm.nosysfs.hint: Without the DRM subsystem there is no way to enumerate the graphics cards.
prov.drm.nouveau: nouveau does not publish the card's clocks, power or usage in sysfs.
prov.drm.nouveau.hint: It is the free driver: what a program like this shows of an NVIDIA (clocks, watts, CUDA cores, throttling) comes from NVML, which ships with the proprietary driver. With nouveau you are left with the temperature, the PCIe link and the memory Vulkan reports.
prov.drm.nvidia: The NVIDIA proprietary driver does not publish the card data in sysfs.
prov.drm.nvidia.hint: They are read through NVML, the library the driver itself ships.
prov.hint.drivetemp: the temperature of the SATA drives
prov.hint.spd: the SPD of the {n} modules: XMP profiles, timings and what speed they could run at
prov.hint.spd.caution: It only reads the module's identification chip; it changes no configuration.
prov.hint.superio: fans, board voltages and chipset temperatures
prov.hint.superio.caution: Do not guess the module: every board carries a different chip and loading the wrong one can read garbage. sensors-detect identifies it and says which to load.
prov.hwmon.nochips: No sensor chip is exposed in /sys/class/hwmon.
prov.hwmon.nochips.hint: On Intel the coretemp module enables it; on AMD, k10temp.
prov.hwmon.nocpu: No sensor chip seems to belong to the CPU.
prov.hwmon.novolt: No sensor on this machine publishes the core voltage.
prov.hwmon.novolt.hint: It usually needs the board's Super I/O module (nct6775, nct6683, it87…) or reading the VID through MSR, which requires root.
prov.mem.denied: Reading the memory modules was not authorised.
prov.mem.denied.hint: You can try again whenever you like.
prov.mem.smbios: The memory modules are in the SMBIOS table, which the kernel reserves for the administrator.
prov.mem.smbios.hint: With permissions you see manufacturer, part number, type, speed, ranks, voltage and how many slots are free.
prov.mem.smbiosfail: Could not read the SMBIOS table: {error}
prov.msr.nomodule: The «msr» module is missing, and core voltage needs it.
prov.msr.novolt: Core voltage lives in the processor, not in a board sensor.
prov.msr.novolt.hint: It is read from a processor register, and the kernel reserves that for the administrator.
prov.msr.nox86: Core voltage is read from a register that only exists on x86.
prov.msr.nox86.hint: On this architecture either the board sensor publishes it or nobody does.
prov.procfs.nostat: There is no /proc/stat on this system.
prov.rapl.denied: The RAPL energy counter exists but cannot be read.
prov.rapl.denied.hint: Many distributions have restricted it to root since CVE-2020-8694.
prov.rapl.none: This CPU exposes no RAPL energy counters.
prov.rapl.none.hint: Normal on older AMD, on ARM and in virtual machines.
prov.spd.unsupported: The SPD of {tipos} cannot be decoded yet.
prov.spd.unsupported.hint: The DDR4 and DDR5 formats are implemented.
prov.sys.nomeminfo: There is no /proc/meminfo on this system.
sensors.alarm.crit: ⚠  It has reached the critical threshold. That is where the machine starts protecting itself.
sensors.alarm.high: ⚠  Above the high threshold. Not a fault, but worth knowing.
sensors.col.name: Sensor
sensors.driver.title: A sensor driver is missing
sensors.header.tip:
Click a column to sort by it; click again to go back to
the order by device.
Drag the dividers to adjust the width.
Right-click to go back to automatic widths.
sensors.limit.estimated: This sensor does not publish its limits: the ones above are silux's estimate from the chip it is, and they err on the safe side.
sensors.tip.record:
Writes one row per sample with every sensor.
It opens in any spreadsheet, and it is how you find out
what minute something happened when you were not watching.
sensors.tip.reset:
Starts counting the extremes again from this moment.
Useful right before launching a load test.
sensors.tip.search:
Filters by sensor or device name.
“memory”, “9070”, “fan”…

settings.accent.help: The colour used to highlight values, charts and the open section.
settings.accent.label: Accent colour
settings.allflags.help: By default only the flags that matter are listed. Turned on, all 53 that CPUID reports on this machine show up.
settings.allflags.label: Show every instruction set
settings.db.counts:
{intel} Intel processors · {amd} AMD · {arm} ARM parts · {sockets} packages.
Built from libcpuid {commit} ({fecha}) and CPU-X {cpux}.
Update it with:  python3 tools/gen_cpu_db.py
settings.db.none:
No database has been generated, so the codename and the package cannot be identified.
Generate it with:  python3 tools/gen_cpu_db.py
settings.density.help: Spacious leaves more room between rows and columns; compact tightens things up to fit more on the same screen.
settings.density.label: Density
settings.fluid.help: Lines glide instead of jumping. It changes no reading at all: it just redraws more often, and costs 2% of one core. Press space to freeze what is on screen.
settings.fluid.label: Smooth chart motion
settings.fontsize.help: Scales up every bit of text. Cards and columns grow with it so nothing gets clipped.
settings.fontsize.label: Text size
settings.interval.help: Every reading walks sysfs and hwmon. Below half a second the cost starts to show; above two, the charts lose detail.
settings.interval.label: Refresh every
settings.language.help: Spanish is the original: when a phrase has not been translated yet, it shows in Spanish rather than blank.
settings.language.label: Language
settings.netunit.help: The same traffic is either 116 MB/s or 931 Mb/s. Speed tests and providers use bits; download managers use bytes.
settings.netunit.label: Network speed
settings.report.button: Save a report of this machine…
settings.tempunit.label: Temperature unit
settings.theme.label: Theme
settings.tip.report:
Generates a text file with all the detected hardware and, above all, with what could not be read and why. It is what to attach when reporting a bug.

It leaves out the machine name, the IP and MAC addresses and the serial numbers.
share.failed: The image could not be saved
share.footer: Made with silux · no identifying data included
share.tip:
An image summarising this machine, ready to paste into a chat or a forum.
It carries no hostname, addresses or serial numbers.
spd.nobus: The SMBus controller exists but the kernel has not enabled it: the board firmware keeps that bus to itself.
spd.nobus.hint: It can be asked to give way by adding acpi_enforce_resources=lax to the kernel boot parameters. It is what lm-sensors and decode-dimms do for the same thing.
spd.nodriver: The bus is there, but the SPD chips have no driver to read them.
spd.nodriver.hint:
Depending on the memory the machine carries:
  sudo modprobe spd5118    (DDR5)
  sudo modprobe ee1004     (DDR4)
  sudo modprobe at24       (DDR3 and earlier)
spd.nosmbus: This board exposes no SMBus controller, which is the bus the modules' SPD chips are read over.
spd.nosmbus.hint: Happens on laptops and on boards where the firmware keeps it to itself. There is no way to read it from the system.
status.blocked.action: {n} value needs permissions — click to grant
status.blocked.action.many: {n} values need permissions — click to grant
status.blocked.tip:
The kernel keeps some data for the administrator: memory module details, disk health and processor power draw.
They are requested once and read without changing anything.
storage.health.body: Power-on hours, terabytes written and wear are kept by each drive in its own diagnostic counters. The kernel reserves those commands for the administrator because they are the same ones used to erase a drive.
storage.health.hint: The helper that gets launched only knows how to ask for diagnostics and read a few system tables: it runs no commands and writes nothing.
storage.health.read: Diagnostics read from {n} of {total} drives. The rest do not publish them or did not answer.
storage.subtitle: {tam} used across {n} mounted partitions
storage.tip.kind: No field states it: it is worked out from whether the kernel considers the drive rotational and which bus it hangs off.
storage.tip.life: What the drive itself reckons it has left, according to its own wear counter.
storage.tip.physical: Modern drives work in 4 KB sectors internally even while telling the system they are 512 B.
storage.tip.scheduler: How the kernel orders requests before sending them to the drive. On an NVMe it is usually off because the drive itself does it better.
storage.tip.written: The TBW: how much data has been written to this drive since it left the factory. It is what consumes an SSD's life.
storage.title: {tam} across {n} drives
storage.warn.hint: The drive itself says so in its diagnostic log. Worth having a copy of whatever is inside.
sys.kernel.name: Kernel
sys.subtitle: {equipo} · up {tiempo}
sys.tip.apps: Total minus free, buffers and reclaimable cache. It comes out slightly below «Used» because that one includes what cannot be given back.
sys.tip.cache: Reclaimable disk cache: Cached + SReclaimable − Shmem.
sys.tip.used: Total minus available. Free alone is not subtracted because on Linux the kernel uses every spare byte as cache, and gives it back the moment something asks for it.
throttle.unknown: a reason it does not report
